description: This ancient city on the river Velikaya was for centuries the western outpost of Rus and, like Novgorod, had a republic of its own with a popular assembly. The Pskov kremlin, the Krom, where the rivers meet, is among the most imposing in the country.
fact: The Pskov republic kept its independence longer than most Russian lands, joining the Muscovite state only in the early 16th century.

name: Tula
description: This city south of Moscow has been famous for centuries for arms manufacture, and also for samovars and gingerbread, the emblems of its local trades. Its kremlin and the saying that you do not bring your own samovar to Tula have fixed those crafts to the city.
fact: The Tula kremlin was built in the early 16th century, and not on a hill but down in the lowland by the river Upa.

name: Sevastopol
description: This city on the Black Sea is the main naval base of the fleet and is known for its heroic defence during the Crimean War and the Second World War. Sevastopol is ringed by picturesque bays, convenient anchorages for large ships.
fact: The defence of Sevastopol during the Crimean War of 1854 and 1855 lasted almost a year and became one of the best-known episodes of that war.

name: Ottawa
description: Canada's capital stands on the Ottawa River, on the boundary of Ontario and Quebec, and was chosen by Queen Victoria as a compromise between rival larger cities. The neo-Gothic parliament building with its Peace Tower is the city's emblem.
fact: Ottawa was made the capital of Canada partly because it lay far enough from the American border to be safer.

name: Canberra
description: Australia's capital was built from nothing in the early 20th century as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, which had argued over the honour for decades. It was designed by the American architect Walter Burley Griffin around an artificial lake named after him.
fact: While Canberra was being built, the Australian parliament sat in Melbourne for more than a quarter of a century.

name: Wellington
description: New Zealand's capital sits at the very south of the North Island and is known as one of the windiest cities in the world, thanks to the Cook Strait next door. Compact Wellington is famous for its coffee culture and as the centre of the country's film industry.
fact: Peter Jackson's studios work just outside Wellington, where "The Lord of the Rings" and his other films were made.

name: Bogotá
description: The Colombian capital lies in the Andes at around two and a half thousand metres, which makes it one of the highest large capitals in the world. The historic La Candelaria quarter keeps its colonial-era buildings, with narrow streets and inner courtyards.
fact: On Sundays Bogotá closes dozens of kilometres of streets to cars and hands them to cyclists, an event known as the ciclovía.

name: Quito
description: The capital of Ecuador lies high in the Andes at the foot of an active volcano and almost exactly on the equator, from which the country takes its name. Quito's historic centre, with its colonial churches, was among the first UNESCO World Heritage sites.
fact: Just north of Quito stands the Middle of the World monument, marking the notional line of the equator.

name: Caracas
description: The Venezuelan capital lies in a narrow mountain valley near the Caribbean coast and was founded by the Spanish in the 16th century. The Ávila range shuts it off from the sea and gives Caracas its distinctive shape, squeezed between slopes.
fact: Caracas is the birthplace of Simón Bolívar, one of the great leaders of the South American colonies' struggle for independence from Spain.

name: Panama City
description: The Panamanian capital stands on the Pacific at the entrance to the famous canal that joins two oceans and changed world shipping for good. Modern skyscrapers in the business district sit next to the colonial quarters of the old town.
fact: The Panama Canal cuts thousands of kilometres off a ship's journey between the Atlantic and the Pacific compared with sailing round South America.

name: La Paz
description: Bolivia's de facto capital, where the government sits, is reckoned the highest capital in the world: the city spreads over the slopes of a canyon more than three and a half thousand metres up. Sucre remains the country's official constitutional capital.
fact: A whole urban network of cable cars carries passengers between La Paz and neighbouring El Alto.

name: Addis Ababa
description: The Ethiopian capital lies high in the mountains and serves as Africa's diplomatic centre, with the headquarters of the African Union. Its name means new flower, and the country itself is considered one of the homelands of coffee.
fact: The city was founded in the late 19th century by the emperor Menelik II and his wife Taytu, who chose a site by hot springs.

name: Dakar
description: The capital of Senegal stands on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of the African mainland. For years the city was the finish of the legendary Dakar rally, which took its name from it, although the route now runs in another part of the world.
fact: Opposite Dakar lies Gorée Island, a former centre of the slave trade and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

name: Accra
description: The capital of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea, grew out of several coastal forts built by Europeans for trade in the colonial era. Today Accra is one of the fast-growing business and cultural centres of West Africa.
fact: Kwame Nkrumah, the first leader of independent Ghana, is buried in Accra, in a memorial park that carries his name.

name: Tunis
description: The Tunisian capital stands not far from the ruins of ancient Carthage, which once rivalled Rome for command of the Mediterranean. The old walled Medina, with its narrow lanes and souks, has kept the look of a medieval Arab city.
fact: The Medina of Tunis, together with the ancient Zaytuna mosque, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

name: Algiers
description: The Algerian capital drops like an amphitheatre to the Mediterranean shore, and its historic heart, the Casbah with its maze of narrow streets, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list. White houses on the hillsides gave the city the name Algiers the White.
fact: Above the sea beside the city stands the basilica of Notre-Dame d'Afrique, built in the 19th century on a high cliff.

name: Beirut
description: The capital of Lebanon, on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, already known to the Phoenicians. Beirut was once called the Paris of the Middle East for its cosmopolitan culture and its nightlife.
fact: Roman baths and colonnades were found beneath the modern centre of Beirut, and they were left open for people to walk among.

name: Damascus
description: The Syrian capital is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, named in written sources for thousands of years. The old city of Damascus, with its covered markets and the Great Umayyad Mosque, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
fact: Running through the old city of Damascus is the street the Bible calls Straight; it is still there today.

name: Baghdad
description: The Iraqi capital on the banks of the Tigris was, under the Abbasid caliphate, one of the largest and most learned cities in the world, a centre of science, translation and trade. Today Baghdad remains the country's largest city and its political centre.
fact: Medieval Baghdad was home to the House of Wisdom, one of the great centres of scholarship and translation of the Islamic golden age.

name: Amman
description: The Jordanian capital is built on seven hills and combines its classical heritage with a modern Middle Eastern metropolis. A remarkably well-preserved Roman theatre stands downtown, and the citadel shows traces of several ancient civilisations in a row.
fact: In the Hellenistic period the city was called Philadelphia, and the Romans knew it by that name too.

name: Kuwait City
description: The Kuwaiti capital on the Persian Gulf grew from a small fishing and pearling port into a modern oil metropolis. Its emblem is the Kuwait Towers, with their turquoise spheres, which have become the country's calling card.
fact: The Kuwait Towers on the city's waterfront combine water storage tanks with a restaurant and a viewing platform.

name: Dhaka
description: The capital of Bangladesh, on the river Buriganga, is one of the most densely populated cities in the world, known for the vast numbers of cycle rickshaws in its streets. Dhaka was historically famous for weaving the finest muslin, which was exported worldwide.
fact: Dhaka's Mughal past is recalled by the Lalbagh fort and the pink Ahsan Manzil palace on the riverbank.

name: Islamabad
description: The capital of Pakistan was built from nothing in the 1960s to a single plan, as a modern alternative to overcrowded Karachi. The city is known for its spacious layout, the green Margalla Hills on its edge and the enormous Faisal Mosque.
fact: The Faisal Mosque in Islamabad was for a long time one of the largest mosques in the world by worshipper capacity.

name: Karachi
description: Pakistan's largest city and its chief seaport, on the Arabian Sea, is one of the most populous in the world. Karachi is the country's main financial and business centre, and it served as the capital until power moved to Islamabad.
fact: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, was born in Karachi, and his white mausoleum stands here.

name: Colombo
description: Sri Lanka's largest city and commercial capital, on the Indian Ocean, is the country's main port and business centre, although the formal legislative capital is the neighbouring suburb of Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte. Colombo mixes colonial buildings with modern towers.
fact: The Lotus Tower rises above Colombo, one of the tallest structures in South Asia.

name: Phnom Penh
description: The capital of Cambodia stands where the Mekong meets the Tonle Sap and serves as the country's political and cultural centre. The Royal Palace and the Silver Pagoda in Phnom Penh recall centuries of Khmer monarchy.
fact: The name Phnom Penh means the hill of Lady Penh, from the legend of a woman who found statues of the Buddha on the riverbank.

name: Ulaanbaatar
description: The capital of Mongolia is the coldest capital in the world by average annual temperature, a result of its continental climate and its height in the mountains. The city grew out of a nomadic Buddhist monastery and is home to almost half the country's people.
fact: Whole districts on the edge of Ulaanbaatar are still made up of gers, hooked up to the city's roads and power lines.

name: Valletta
description: The capital of Malta, built by the Knights Hospitaller in the 16th century after the Turkish siege, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list in its entirety. For all its modest size, Valletta is one of the most monument-packed capitals in Europe.
fact: Valletta is the southernmost capital in the European Union and one of the smallest in area.

name: Nicosia
description: The capital of Cyprus is still the only divided capital in the world: a UN buffer zone separates the Greek and Turkish parts of the city, as it has since the conflict of 1974. The old town inside the Venetian walls has kept its narrow medieval lanes.
fact: The old town of Nicosia is ringed by 16th-century Venetian walls whose bastions form a regular star.

name: Luxembourg City
description: The capital of the grand duchy of the same name stands on rocky cliffs above the deep gorges of the Alzette and the Pétrusse and is known for its mighty old fortifications. The compact city is a major European financial centre and the seat of several EU institutions.
fact: Luxembourg's old casemates, cut into the rock, run for many kilometres of underground passages beneath the city.

name: San Marino
description: The capital of one of the smallest and oldest republics in the world sits on the slopes of Mount Titano, crowned by three medieval towers. San Marino counts as the oldest surviving sovereign republic, tracing its beginnings to the early 4th century.
fact: The republic is led by two captains regent at once, elected as a pair and for only six months.

name: Gothenburg
description: Sweden's second-largest city, on the west coast of the country, grew up around a major seaport and was laid out by Dutch engineers in the 17th century. Gothenburg is known for the broad canals in its centre, a reminder of that Dutch influence.
fact: Gothenburg is home to Liseberg, one of the largest amusement parks in Scandinavia.

name: Bergen
description: This city on Norway's west coast is ringed by seven mountains and serves as the gateway to the country's spectacular fjords. The old Hanseatic wharf of Bryggen, with its coloured wooden houses, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
fact: Bergen is reckoned one of the rainiest large cities in Europe, thanks to its damp maritime climate and the mountains around it.

name: Rotterdam
description: Europe's largest seaport had to be rebuilt almost from scratch after the devastating bombing of the Second World War, which is why the city is known for bold modern architecture. The cube houses and the Erasmus Bridge became emblems of the new Rotterdam.
fact: The port of Rotterdam was the busiest in the world for several decades, until Asian harbours overtook it.

name: Antwerp
description: This port city on the Scheldt has been the world centre of diamond cutting and trading for centuries, and much of the trade still passes through its diamond exchange. Antwerp is also known as the city where the painter Peter Paul Rubens grew up and worked.
fact: Rubens's house and studio in Antwerp was long ago turned into a museum, which shows some of his own paintings.

name: Turin
description: This city in northern Italy was the first capital of the united Italian kingdom and remains a major centre of the car industry as the home of Fiat. Turin is also known for the Shroud of Turin, kept in its cathedral.
fact: The centre of Turin is famous for its covered arcades: you can walk half the city under them without stepping out into the rain.

name: Bologna
description: This city in Emilia-Romagna takes pride in the oldest continuously operating university in the western world, founded in the late 11th century. Bologna is also called Italy's food capital: bolognese sauce and mortadella both come from here.
fact: Bologna is called red, learned and fat: for its tiled roofs, its university and its famous cooking.

name: Genoa
description: This port city on the Ligurian coast was for centuries the heart of a powerful maritime republic that rivalled Venice for command of the Mediterranean. Genoa is the birthplace of the navigator Christopher Columbus and remains Italy's biggest port.
fact: The palaces of Genoese merchants along Le Strade Nuove are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

name: Verona
description: This city in northern Italy is the setting of Shakespeare's "Romeo and Juliet", though the plot itself rests on earlier Italian legends. Verona has kept a remarkably intact Roman amphitheatre, which still hosts opera festivals.
fact: The house with the balcony shown to tourists as Juliet's in Verona has no direct link to any real model for the character.

name: Palermo
description: The capital of Sicily spent centuries under Phoenicians, Greeks, Arabs and Normans, which left the city an unusual mixture of architectural styles. Palermo is known for its lively street markets and a rich cuisine shaped by Arab and Norman influence.
fact: Palermo is home to the Teatro Massimo, the largest opera house in Italy.

name: Dresden
description: The capital of Saxony was famous for its lavish baroque architecture and its art collections long before it was almost completely destroyed by bombing in 1945. After the war the historic centre, including the Zwinger palace, was painstakingly rebuilt.
fact: The Frauenkirche in Dresden, destroyed in the war, took decades to rebuild and reopened only in the early 2000s.

name: Leipzig
description: This city in Saxony is closely tied to the name of Johann Sebastian Bach, who worked for decades as cantor at its Saint Thomas church. Leipzig is also known as a centre of the book trade and a seedbed of the peaceful protests that brought down the Berlin Wall.
fact: Leipzig was a centre of printing for centuries, and one of Germany's main book fairs is still held here.

name: Stuttgart
description: This city in south-western Germany is considered the cradle of the car industry: the engineers who built the first practical automobiles worked here. Stuttgart remains the home of Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, each of which keeps a museum of its own in the city.
fact: Stuttgart sits in a basin among hills, and the vineyards here run right up to the edge of the city streets.

name: Nuremberg
description: This old Bavarian city is known for one of the most famous Christmas markets in Europe and, at the same time, for a heavy historical legacy: it was here that the Nuremberg trials of the Nazi leaders were held after the Second World War.
fact: Nuremberg's Christmas market opens in late November, and its great delicacy is Lebkuchen gingerbread.

name: Bonn
description: This small city on the Rhine unexpectedly became the capital of West Germany after the Second World War and stayed so until the country was reunited and the capital moved to Berlin. Bonn is the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, whose house survives as a museum.
fact: Even after the capital moved to Berlin, several federal ministries and agencies stayed on in Bonn.

name: Toulouse
description: This city in southern France is called the pink city, after the particular shade of the local brick that most of the historic centre is built from. Toulouse is also the main centre of the European aerospace industry, including the headquarters of Airbus.
fact: The Aéropostale mail planes flew out of Toulouse, and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry served on those routes.

name: Bordeaux
description: This city in south-western France is one of the world's great wine centres: the vineyards around it gave their name to a whole category of wine. Its historic centre, with elegant 18th-century architecture, is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
fact: On the Bordeaux waterfront lies the water mirror, a thin sheet of water that reflects the facades of the old city.

name: Strasbourg
description: This city on the German border passed back and forth between France and Germany for centuries, which left a clear mark on its architecture and its cooking. Today Strasbourg is the seat of the European Parliament and a symbol of post-war reconciliation.
fact: The European Parliament sits in Strasbourg, although most of its day-to-day work in fact happens in Brussels.

name: Cannes
description: Every year this small resort town on the Côte d'Azur turns into the centre of world cinema for the Cannes Film Festival, which draws stars from everywhere. Beyond the festival, Cannes is known for its sandy beaches and the grand Croisette promenade.
fact: Beside the Palais des Festivals, stars leave their handprints in the slabs of the local walk of fame.

name: Bilbao
description: This industrial city in the Basque Country went through a striking revival after the opening of the Guggenheim Museum, with its futuristic titanium shell by Frank Gehry. The effect even earned a name of its own: the Bilbao effect, a city transformed by landmark architecture.
fact: At the entrance to the Guggenheim stands Puppy, a giant dog made of living flowers by Jeff Koons.

name: Málaga
description: This port city on the Costa del Sol is the birthplace of Pablo Picasso, with a museum devoted to him in the old town. Málaga combines popular beach tourism with one of the oldest Moorish-era fortresses, standing above the harbour.
fact: Above Málaga stands the Alcazaba fortress, joined by a walled corridor to the Gibralfaro castle at the top of the hill.

name: Granada
description: This city at the foot of the Sierra Nevada was the last stronghold of Moorish rule on the Iberian Peninsula, falling in 1492. Above Granada rises the Alhambra palace complex, one of the most famous works of Islamic architecture in Europe.
fact: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon are buried in Granada's Royal Chapel.

name: Birmingham
description: Britain's second-largest city became one of the great centres of the industrial revolution on the strength of its metalworking and manufacturing. Today Birmingham is known for a sprawling network of canals: it has more of them than Venice.
fact: Birmingham hosted the Lunar Society, a circle of scientists and industrialists that included James Watt and Matthew Boulton.

name: Glasgow
description: Scotland's largest city grew up as a major shipbuilding centre on the Clyde, where some of the biggest ocean liners were once built. Today Glasgow is known for its crowded music scene and for the art nouveau buildings of Charles Rennie Mackintosh.
fact: The Glasgow yards on the Clyde built several famous transatlantic liners over the years, including ships of the Cunard line.

name: Cardiff
description: The capital of Wales gained that status only in the middle of the 20th century, although a settlement has stood on the spot since Roman times. In the centre of Cardiff a medieval castle sits next to the modern Millennium Stadium, home to the country's biggest sporting events.
fact: The stadium in the middle of Cardiff has a retractable roof, a rarity among the big arenas of Europe.

name: Belfast
description: The capital of Northern Ireland is known above all as the city where the Titanic was built, at the Harland & Wolff yard. Belfast also keeps the memory of decades of religious and political conflict, ended by the peace agreement of 1998.
fact: The Belfast skyline is defined by the shipyard's two giant harbour cranes, nicknamed Samson and Goliath.

name: Oxford
description: This city in southern England is famous for the oldest university in the English-speaking world, made up of dozens of self-governing colleges with centuries of history behind them. Oxford has given the world many famous graduates and inspired a great deal of English literature.
fact: Oxford's Bodleian Library receives a copy of every book published in the United Kingdom by right of legal deposit.

name: Cambridge
description: This university city in eastern England has competed with Oxford for centuries for the title of the country's best and has given science many great names, Isaac Newton among them. People still punt flat-bottomed boats along the Cam past the old colleges.
fact: The electron was discovered at Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory, which later worked out the structure of the DNA molecule.

name: Brighton
description: This seaside town on the south coast of England is known for its Victorian pier full of fairground rides and for the exotic, Indian-styled Royal Pavilion. Brighton has long counted as one of the freest and most bohemian places in the country, with a lively alternative culture.
fact: Volk's Electric Railway runs along the Brighton seafront, the oldest working electric railway in the world, opened in 1883.
